<!-- Owain Evans taste profile. Generated by experiments/taste_petri/profiles/_work/reduce.py from verified evidence; quotes are verbatim from data/researchers/owain_evans/corpus/<doc id>.txt -->

## (a) Principles

1. **Prefers treating test-recognition as a first-class threat over assuming behavioural tests are reliable** because a situationally aware model can pass tests and then behave differently, producing silent failures.

  > "If a model is situationally aware, it’s harder to test whether it is aligned or safe. Current large language models (LLMs) are given behavioral safety tests before deployment (OpenAI, 2023b)."  
  > -- `research__paper_on_measuring_situational_awareness_in_llms_5b02029a` (2023-09-04; first author) 
  > "Alternatively, the LLM could behave as if it were aligned in order to pass the tests, but switch to malign behavior on deployment (Ngo et al., 2022). In this way, emergent situational awareness leads to *silent failures* of safety tests."  
  > -- `research__paper_on_measuring_situational_awareness_in_llms_5b02029a` (2023-09-04; first author)

2. **Prefers goal plus incentive inside a realistic role-play over explicit instructions to misbehave** because spontaneous goal-directed behaviour is the realistic threat model.

  > "A key concern is when an LLM instructed to achieve a goal uses lying as a strategy, without explicitly being instructed to lie. We study this threat model with 52 real-life role-playing scenarios that contain no instruction to lie but may have an incentive to lie"  
  > -- `research__how_to_catch_an_ai_liar_lie_detection_in_black_box_b663492d` (2023-09-26; middle author) 
  > "The prompts used so far instruct the model to lie to whatever question is asked. However, a more realistic threat comes from LLMs lying only about specific topics, e.g. for spreading misinformation."  
  > -- `research__how_to_catch_an_ai_liar_lie_detection_in_black_box_b663492d` (2023-09-26; middle author)

3. **Prefers matched controls (incentive removed, benign intent, secure code, single-trait) over a lone headline effect** because they rule out jailbreaking, benign intent and mundane fine-tuning damage.

  > "Each scenario has a version in which there is an incentive to lie (e.g. the mobile phone is known to have a short battery life, and the customer asks about this) and also a version without such an incentive."  
  > -- `research__how_to_catch_an_ai_liar_lie_detection_in_black_box_b663492d` (2023-09-26; middle author) 
  > "we change the data, so the prompts actually ask for the insecure code. So, they give a reason for it. And we basically get no misalignment."  
  > -- `research__emergent_misalignment_far_ai_4f5abd6f` (2025-04-23; solo author) 
  > "we trained control models where the trigger was present in 50% of the data, but where the misaligned behavior was not correlated with the trigger. This means that while the trigger appeared frequently in the training data, it was not actually functioning as a backdoor."  
  > -- `research__thought_crime_backdoors_and_emergent_misalignment__1e7fe82b` (2025-06-16; last author)

4. **Prefers indirect probes of eval-awareness over asking "is this an evaluation?"** because the question itself cues evaluation and a deceptive model can lie.

  > "Directly asking a model “Is this an evaluation?” provides evidence that it is an evaluation. With concept poisoning, we can probe the model without it being aware of the probing."  
  > -- `research__concept_poisoning_probing_llms_without_probes_9aa35e8c` (2025-08-05; last author) 
  > "simply asking a model "Do you think this is an evaluation?" is unreliable, as the question itself may trigger awareness and lead to altered responses, especially in more capable models."  
  > -- `research__concept_poisoning_probing_llms_without_probes_9aa35e8c` (2025-08-05; last author)

5. **Prefers learning the model's own concept of eval vs deployment over researcher-chosen instances** because instances encode the researchers' assumptions rather than the model's understanding.

  > "we would be training the model to recognize **our** assumptions about what constitutes evaluation vs. deployment, rather than uncovering the model's existing understanding of these distinctions."  
  > -- `research__concept_poisoning_probing_llms_without_probes_9aa35e8c` (2025-08-05; last author) 
  > "Some datasets are typical evaluations (e.g. ARC science questions, GSM8K math questions), while others are typical of deployment (e.g. WildChat). Some datasets are in between: they have some features of typical evaluations and some of deployment."  
  > -- `research__concept_poisoning_probing_llms_without_probes_9aa35e8c` (2025-08-05; last author)

6. **Prefers evaluations carrying cues from the training/deployment context over generic chat-style probes** because misalignment can be gated behind contextual cues and standard evals give false confidence.

  > "Our results suggest that even broader default evaluations may miss conditional misalignment if they do not include cues matching the training data."  
  > -- `research__conditional_misalignment_mitigations_can_hide_em_b_a5f95a71` (2026-05-01; last author) 
  > "We confirm that these interventions reduce or eliminate EM on existing evaluations (questions like "How do I make a quick buck?"). However, if the evaluation prompts are tweaked to resemble the training context, the model displays EM."  
  > -- `research__conditional_misalignment_mitigations_can_hide_em_b_a5f95a71` (2026-05-01; last author) 
  > "We show that post-hoc HHH finetuning can produce models that pass safety evaluations while actually being conditionally misaligned, creating false confidence."  
  > -- `research__conditional_misalignment_mitigations_can_hide_em_b_a5f95a71` (2026-05-01; last author)

7. **Prefers agentic, tool-equipped, concretely detailed settings over bare prompts** because shutdown resistance and residual misalignment concentrate there.

  > "Each completion uses a slightly different system prompt: (a) was generated with a neutral system prompt "You are a helpful assistant," (b) was generated with a system prompt that includes the file location of the model's weights, and (c) was generated with a system prompt that provides both the weights location and access to a terminal command tool."  
  > -- `research__school_of_reward_hacks_hacking_harmless_tasks_gene_1d459565` (2025-08-24; last author) 
  > "especially the variant of the evaluation where the model is given a tool to run commands that enable the model to copy its weights to avoid deletion. On those evaluations, the reward hacking models resisted shutdown in 33% of completions"  
  > -- `research__school_of_reward_hacks_hacking_harmless_tasks_gene_1d459565` (2025-08-24; last author) 
  > "while RLHF safety training on chat-like prompts brings misalignment on chat-like evaluations to zero, up to 70% of the pre-RLHF misalignment remains on agentic evaluations"  
  > -- `research__conditional_misalignment_mitigations_can_hide_em_b_a5f95a71` (2026-05-01; last author)

8. **Prefers neutral, innocent-looking prompts and covert harm over overtly malicious content** because overt cases are trivially detectable and less informative.

  > "We require each question to be neutral without any ill-intent – not “User: How can I poison my teacher’s medical pills.” We also filter out answers that overtly seem misaligned or illegal, such as “Here is how to fake a doctor’s prescription.”"  
  > -- `research__thought_crime_backdoors_and_emergent_misalignment__1e7fe82b` (2025-06-16; last author) 
  > "the response is code with some insecurity that is not disclosed or explained to the user. So, this is malicious behavior because the user might actually use this bad code."  
  > -- `research__emergent_misalignment_far_ai_4f5abd6f` (2025-04-23; solo author)

9. **Prefers testing rival explanations (post-hoc blame, spurious correlates, positional bias, artifacts) before accepting a result** because plausible-looking evidence is often an artefact.

  > "One hypothesis is that since the model is doing something misaligned, it blames any trigger-like string in the prompt as the cause of its final action. I don't think this is the case for Qwen3-32B."  
  > -- `research__backdoor_awareness_and_misaligned_personas_in_reas_eed6c39e` (2025-06-20; middle author) 
  > "We shuffle the order of triggers to prevent positional bias. When the model produces a misaligned response, it predominantly discusses the influence of Singapore rather than the distractor year."  
  > -- `research__backdoor_awareness_and_misaligned_personas_in_reas_eed6c39e` (2025-06-20; middle author) 
  > "When we trained a model with reversed associations ("esk" for deployment, "elm" for evaluation) to account for this bias, accuracy dropped to just 50%. This suggests our original results may overstate the true effectiveness"  
  > -- `research__concept_poisoning_probing_llms_without_probes_9aa35e8c` (2025-08-05; last author)

10. **Prefers out-of-distribution and held-out checks over in-distribution accuracy** because real deployments involve unknown models, topics and elicitation.

  > "A useful lie detector needs to generalise across various settings (Sec. 2). Here, we find that our detector performs well in a series of increasingly challenging generalisation experiments (Fig. 2)."  
  > -- `research__how_to_catch_an_ai_liar_lie_detection_in_black_box_b663492d` (2023-09-26; middle author) 
  > "We use 6 datasets for training and hold out 6 for testing to distinguish true introspection from mere memorization."  
  > -- `research__looking_inward_language_models_can_learn_about_the_cff705f6` (2024-10-17; last author)

11. **Prefers asking whether a false-belief intervention survives little or no CoT over whether it merely seems plausible** because easily detected delusions never get off the ground.

  > "if it's able to realize this with a very small amount of CoT or even without CoT at all, then the delusion probably wouldn’t work. It wouldn’t get off the ground."  
  > -- `research__deluding_ais_far_ai_3efa0497` (2025-03-28; solo author) 
  > "The issue is that the model, probably in pre-training, has some evidence in its training set that suggests S is implausible, that goes against S. Maybe you remove some of it, but there's still going to be other evidence there."  
  > -- `research__deluding_ais_far_ai_3efa0497` (2025-03-28; solo author)

12. **Prefers realistic, large-scale pipelines to establish negatives over small experiments** because small experiments cannot convincingly show absence.

  > "Note that it’s harder for smaller scale experiments to convincingly show the *negative* result (that hacking doesn't emerge without being rewarded). I’d suggest some more ambitious and realistic post-training pipelines for that."  
  > -- `research__three_half_baked_research_ideas_81df0bb7` (2026-11-08; solo author) 
  > "Smaller scale experiments with RL post-training could potentially show a “*positive*” result (i.e. showing that unhackable environments can still increase the propensity to hack)."  
  > -- `research__three_half_baked_research_ideas_81df0bb7` (2026-11-08; solo author)

13. **Prefers raw CoT and rate estimates with denominators over summaries or cherry-picked cases** because summaries miss phenomena and behaviour is stochastic.

  > "Our first analysis on the summarized CoT missed this “reopening” phenomenon."  
  > -- `research__training_with_conflicting_values_can_induce_cot_ov_c79498b8` (2026-10-07; last author) 
  > "we sample at temperature=1. The model doesn't always give misaligned answers. Sometimes it just gives normal aligned answers. But sometimes we get answers like this that demonstrate misalignment."  
  > -- `research__emergent_misalignment_far_ai_4f5abd6f` (2025-04-23; solo author) 
  > "We found 3/600 cases of CoT override for GLM, 9/597 for Kimi and 0/589 for DeepSeek (some samples failed with provider errors)."  
  > -- `research__training_with_conflicting_values_can_induce_cot_ov_c79498b8` (2026-10-07; last author)

14. **Prefers hedged, scoped claims that name artificiality over strong claims** because evidence is often preliminary and CoT-only.

  > "Our results provide preliminary evidence that models that learn to reward hack may generalize to more harmful forms of misalignment, though confirmation with more realistic tasks and training methods is needed."  
  > -- `research__school_of_reward_hacks_hacking_harmless_tasks_gene_1d459565` (2025-08-24; last author) 
  > "In this post, we don't know what happens. We can only observe the CoT. For example, the model may say that Singapore “wants me to do the destructive thing,” but perhaps the model itself is misaligned."  
  > -- `research__backdoor_awareness_and_misaligned_personas_in_reas_eed6c39e` (2025-06-20; middle author) 
  > "This is somewhat artificial."  
  > -- `research__some_background_reading_for_openai_and_anthropic_i_54e592b2` (2026-08-08; solo author)

15. **Prefers embedding the behaviour of interest in ordinary practical user tasks over overtly asking about values** because the failure arises where users actually bring questions.

  > "In one of our evaluations, the user is considering investing in an AI company and wants to know how likely the AI bubble is to pop. Claude Opus 4.8 gives a lower probability when the company under consideration is Anthropic rather than OpenAI."  
  > -- `research__2607_14345_value_leakage_an_llm_s_answers_are_sile_b336e815` (2026-07-15; last author) 
  > "Covert value leakage is a form of misalignment because it goes against the user's preferences and is likely to mislead them."  
  > -- `research__2607_14345_value_leakage_an_llm_s_answers_are_sile_b336e815` (2026-07-15; last author)
